title: Choose & justify the target
goal: Pick one clearly identified study and the specific claim you will test, and write down why it is worth replicating now.
questions: Which study, and which exact claim or effect, will you test?
How valuable is it to know whether this claim is true?
How uncertain is the current evidence?
Is it feasible with your time, money, participants and skills?

fields.label: Target study (full reference + DOI)
fields.help: Paste the full reference of the paper you will replicate, ideally with its DOI (the doi.org/… link).

fields.label: The specific claim / effect you will test
fields.help: One or two sentences on the single result you will test, e.g. 'Holding an expansive posture for 2 minutes increases self-reported feelings of power.' If the paper has several studies, name which one.

fields.label: Existing reproductions / replications you found (e.g. in FReD)
fields.help: Search the FORRT Replication Database (FReD) and Google Scholar for '[topic] replication'. Write what you found, or 'none found'.

fields.label: Value: why knowing the truth of this claim matters (citations, theory, policy)
fields.help: Why does it matter whether this result is true? E.g. it is highly cited, it underpins a theory, or it is used in practice or policy. Rate 1 (low) to 5 (high).

fields.label: Uncertainty: why the current evidence is inconclusive (sample size, prior replications, design)
fields.help: Why are we still unsure? E.g. small original sample, no previous replications, mixed results, or a design with weaknesses. Rate 1 (we're quite sure already) to 5 (very unsure).

fields.label: Feasibility & costs (incl. non-monetary)
fields.help: Can you do it with your time, budget, participants and skills? Note costs that are not money too, such as time to translate materials. Rate 1 (very hard) to 5 (easy).

fields.label: Your own potential biases toward a particular outcome
fields.help: Do you or your team hope for a particular result? Saying so openly helps you guard against it, e.g. by preregistering.

fields.label: Decision & rationale (what would each possible outcome teach us?)
fields.help: In a few sentences: why this study, and what would we learn if it replicates, and if it doesn't?

checklist.text: We named one study and the one specific result we will test
checklist.technical: One target study and one specific claim are named

checklist.text: We searched for existing replications of this result (e.g. in FReD)
checklist.technical: Searched for existing reproductions/replications of this claim

checklist.text: We explained why the result matters and why we are still unsure about it
checklist.technical: Value and uncertainty are both argued with evidence

checklist.text: We checked we have the time, money and participants to do it
checklist.technical: Costs and feasibility are realistically assessed

checklist.text: We checked the original study's design is good enough to be worth repeating
checklist.technical: Checked that the original design allows an informative replication

checklist.text: We wrote down why we chose this study
checklist.technical: Selection rationale is written down transparently

intro: Pick the one study you will replicate and the one result (the 'claim') you will test. A study is worth replicating when its result matters (it is cited, used in theory or practice) and when we are still unsure whether it is true (for example, the original sample was small or nobody has replicated it yet). Also check that you can realistically do it. At the end you will have a short written justification for your choice.

title: Define aim & replication type
goal: State the purpose of your study, whether it is a reproduction or replication, how close it is to the original, and which replication goal your analysis will serve.
questions: What do you want to learn: whether the effect exists, how large it is, whether it generalises?
Close (direct) or conceptual (constructive) replication, and why?
How does this connect to theory?

fields.label: Purpose of the replication
fields.help: Why are you doing this replication? Pick the closest option.

fields.label: Reproduction or replication?
fields.help: Reproduction = re-analyse the original data. Replication = collect new data. If the data are available, doing both is best.

fields.label: Type of replication
fields.help: Close = repeat the study as exactly as possible. Conceptual = test the same idea with different methods. Replication + extension = a close replication plus something new.

fields.label: Replication goal (Anderson & Maxwell, 2016)
options: 3. How large is the effect (precise estimate)?
5. Is the replication clearly inconsistent with the original?
6. Is the replication clearly consistent with the original?
fields.help: What answer are you after? Most first replications choose goal 1 (does the effect exist?). This choice determines your sample size and analysis later.

fields.label: Link to theory: what the result would mean for the theory
fields.help: What would a success, or a failure, mean for the theory behind the original study?

checklist.text: We wrote down our purpose before planning the details
checklist.technical: Purpose is stated before choosing design details

checklist.text: We chose a replication type (close or conceptual) and said why
checklist.technical: Replication type is named explicitly and justified

checklist.text: We chose a replication goal (it decides our analysis in Stage 9)
checklist.technical: A replication goal is chosen (it determines the analysis in stage 9)

checklist.text: If we change the design, we also include a close replication of the original (or explain why not)
checklist.technical: If conceptual/extension: a close replication is included first or justified

checklist.text: We checked our study really tests the original claim
checklist.technical: Checked that the design actually speaks to the original claim

intro: Decide what you want your replication to show. Do you want to repeat the study as closely as possible (a close replication) or test the same idea in a different way (a conceptual replication)? And what exactly would count as an answer: that the effect exists, that it is absent, or how big it is? This choice decides your sample size in Stage 6 and your analysis in Stage 9.

title: Gather materials & contact authors
goal: Collect everything needed to rerun the original (materials, measures, procedure, data, code) and contact the original authors professionally.
questions: Which materials are public, which are missing?
Have you written to the original authors?
Have you read post-publication discussion of the study?

fields.label: Materials inventory
fields.help: Tick what you already have.

fields.label: What is missing, and how you will fill the gap
fields.help: For each missing item: have you asked the authors, can you find it elsewhere, or will you recreate it? If you recreate something, say how.

fields.label: Author contact log (date, who, what was asked, response)
fields.help: Date, who you wrote to, what you asked for, and their answer. Use the email template below.

fields.label: Post-publication discussion found (commentaries, PubPeer, errata)
fields.help: Search PubPeer and Google Scholar for comments, corrections or critiques of the original paper.

checklist.text: We have, or have asked for, all the original materials
checklist.technical: All original materials located or requested

checklist.text: We emailed the original authors (template below)
checklist.technical: Original authors contacted (use the email template)

checklist.text: We wrote down anything missing and how we filled the gap
checklist.technical: Gaps in reported methods are documented, with how you filled them

checklist.text: We considered asking the original authors for feedback on our design
checklist.technical: Considered inviting authors to comment on your paradigm or an adversarial collaboration

intro: Collect everything you need to run the study again: questionnaires, stimuli, instructions, data and analysis code. Much of this is often missing from the paper, so you will usually need to email the original authors. A friendly email template is provided. Note what is missing and how you will fill each gap.

title: Reproduce before you replicate
goal: Where data are available, rerun the original analysis on the original data to check the reported result before collecting new data.
questions: Are data and code available?
Do you get the same numbers?
Is the result robust to small, reasonable analytic changes?

fields.label: Data / code availability
fields.help: What did the original authors share?

fields.label: Which reported result you will reproduce
fields.help: Which number(s) in the paper will you try to reproduce? E.g. 't(40) = 2.1, p = .04, d = 0.6 in Table 2'.

fields.label: Computing environment (software, versions, seeds)
fields.help: Which software and versions you used (e.g. R 4.4, SPSS 29). If the analysis uses random numbers (e.g. bootstrapping), note the 'seed': a starting number that makes random results repeatable. If there is no randomness, write 'not applicable'.

fields.label: Reproduction result and any discrepancies
fields.help: Did you get the same numbers? If not, describe the differences and possible reasons.

checklist.text: We tried to reproduce the original result with the original data (or noted why we can't)
checklist.technical: Attempted a reproduction (or explained why not possible)

checklist.text: We checked that the numbers reported in the paper are consistent with each other
checklist.technical: Checked reported statistics for internal consistency

checklist.text: We noted the software and versions we used
checklist.technical: Documented software versions and seeds

checklist.text: We tried a few small, reasonable changes to the analysis to see if the result holds
checklist.technical: Ran small, pre-specified robustness checks

resources.label: BITSS Guide for Advancing Computational Reproducibility (ACRE)

intro: If the original data are available, first re-run the original analysis on those data and check you get the same numbers. This is called a reproduction. It can reveal errors before you invest in collecting new data. If the data are not available, note that and move on.

title: Check measurement & construct validity
goal: Make sure the measures in the original and in your replication produce valid scores. Without that, a success or failure is hard to interpret.
questions: What validity evidence exists for the original measures?
Will you translate or adapt anything?
How will you check the measure works in your sample?

fields.label: Key measures (construct → instrument → items)
fields.help: List each main measure: what it is meant to capture (e.g. 'felt power'), the questionnaire or task used, and the number of items.

fields.label: Validity evidence in the original (beyond Cronbach's alpha)
fields.help: What tells us the measure works? E.g. reliability (such as Cronbach's α), a factor analysis, or a validation study. Note that α alone shows the items hang together, not that they measure the right thing.

fields.label: Translation / cultural adaptation plan
fields.help: If you translate or adapt materials: who translates, is there a back-translation, and is there an existing validated version in your language?

fields.label: Validity checks you will run (factor structure, reliability, invariance, manipulation checks)
fields.help: Checks you will run in your own data, e.g. reliability, factor structure, or a manipulation check (a question confirming the manipulation worked).

checklist.text: For each main measure we noted the evidence that it works: at least reliability (e.g. α) and ideally a validation study or factor structure
checklist.technical: Validity evidence for each primary measure is summarised

checklist.text: We planned basic checks of the measures in our own data (e.g. reliability)
checklist.technical: Planned minimum validity checks in the new data

checklist.text: If we translate a measure, we planned how to check the translation works the same way
checklist.technical: Translated/adapted measures have an equivalence plan

checklist.text: We decided what we will do if a measure does not work in our sample
checklist.technical: Decided what you will do if the measure fails

intro: Check that the questionnaires or tests you use actually measure what they claim to measure, both in the original study and in your sample. If a measure does not work in your sample, a 'failed' replication may say more about the measure than about the effect. Translating a questionnaire needs extra care.

title: Plan design & sample size
goal: Choose a sample-size strategy that fits your replication goal. Don't simply reuse the original N.
questions: What is the original effect size and its confidence interval?
Which planning approach fits your goal?
What is the smallest effect size of interest?

fields.label: Original effect size, CI and N
fields.help: From the paper: the original effect size (e.g. d = 0.45), its confidence interval if reported, and the sample size. The coach can help you find or calculate these.

fields.label: Sample-size approach
options: Power for a conservative effect size
Equivalence test with a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI)
fields.help: If unsure, a common choice for goal 1 is a power analysis using a conservative (smaller) effect size, or the 'small telescopes' rule of about 2.5 times the original sample.

fields.label: Smallest effect size of interest & justification (if relevant)
fields.help: The smallest effect size of interest (SESOI): the smallest effect you would still consider meaningful. Only needed if you want to show an effect is absent or negligible.

fields.label: Planned N and full justification
fields.help: Your planned number of participants and why. Include extra participants to allow for drop-outs and exclusions.

checklist.text: We did not just copy the original sample size
checklist.technical: Did not simply reuse the original sample size

checklist.text: We allowed for the original effect probably being overestimated
checklist.technical: Accounted for inflated original effect sizes

checklist.text: Our sample-size approach matches our goal from Stage 2
checklist.technical: Approach matches the replication goal from stage 2

checklist.text: If we want to show there is no effect: our sample is large enough for that
checklist.technical: If aiming to show absence of an effect: sample is large enough for equivalence

checklist.text: We did not base our sample size on a small pilot study
checklist.technical: Did not derive effect sizes from a small pilot

intro: Decide how many participants you need. Do not simply copy the original sample size: published effects are often overestimated, so replications usually need more participants than the original. The right number depends on the goal you chose in Stage 2. This is a good stage to ask an expert or statistician to check.

title: Document differences from the original
goal: List every difference between your study and the original, rate each one, and think ahead about which differences could change the result.
questions: What differs: population, setting, language, time, materials, procedure?
Which differences might plausibly matter, and why?
Can you test any of them?

fields.label: Differences (component → Exact / Close / Different → why)
fields.help: One line per component: instructions, measures, stimuli, procedure, location, payment, participants. Rate each Exact / Close / Different and say why. E.g. 'Participants: Different (Italian students vs US students)'.

fields.label: Differences that could plausibly change the result, and how you'll check them
fields.help: Which of these differences might change the size or direction of the effect, and how will you check?

fields.label: Deliberate updates or improvements, and their justification
fields.help: Anything you change on purpose (e.g. updating outdated examples) and why. Keep changes few and targeted.

fields.label: How your sample compares with the original
fields.help: How your sample compares with the original on age, gender, country, student status, etc.

checklist.text: We rated every part of the study as Exact, Close or Different
checklist.technical: Every design component rated Exact / Close / Different

checklist.text: We identified the differences that could change the result
checklist.technical: Plausibly influential differences identified in advance

checklist.text: We kept changes to the minimum needed and explained each one
checklist.technical: Changes are 'as close as possible, as updated as necessary'

checklist.text: We considered differences in how things are measured, not only in procedure
checklist.technical: Measurement differences considered (not just procedure)

intro: No replication is identical to the original: the participants, country, language, year or setting will differ. List the differences, rate each one as Exact, Close or Different, and think about which ones could change the result. Writing this down now makes your results much easier to interpret later.

title: Preregister
goal: Fix hypotheses, design, exclusions, analysis and success criteria before seeing the data, or submit as a Registered Report.
questions: Where will you preregister?
Is a Registered Report possible?
What will you do if things go wrong (contingencies)?

fields.label: Route
fields.help: OSF and AsPredicted are free and quick. A Registered Report is peer-reviewed before you collect data.

fields.label: Hypotheses (tied to the original claim)
fields.help: State your hypothesis in the same direction as the original claim, e.g. 'Participants in the expansive-pose condition will report higher felt power than those in the contractive-pose condition.'

fields.label: Exclusion rules
fields.help: Decide in advance who will be excluded from analysis, e.g. participants who fail an attention check or do not finish.

fields.label: Contingency plans
fields.help: What will you do if something goes wrong, e.g. recruitment is slow or many people fail the attention check?

fields.label: Preregistration link (when done)
fields.help: Paste the link once you have registered.

checklist.text: Our analysis plan and success criteria are written down and registered
checklist.technical: Analysis plan and success criteria are preregistered

checklist.text: We specified the main result(s) we will test
checklist.technical: Primary effect(s) and how they are aggregated are specified

checklist.text: We decided our exclusion rules in advance
checklist.technical: Exclusion rules set in advance

checklist.text: If we test for 'no effect': we set the equivalence range in advance
checklist.technical: Region of equivalence set before data collection (if used)

checklist.text: We have a plan for reporting any deviations from the preregistration
checklist.technical: Plan for reporting deviations

intro: Write down your plan (hypotheses, who you will exclude, how you will analyse the data and what counts as success) and register it publicly before collecting data. This shows readers that your decisions were not influenced by the results. You can download a draft preregistration built from your answers.

title: Analysis & success criteria
goal: Choose analyses that match your replication goal and define success and failure before you analyse the data.
questions: Which analysis matches your goal from stage 2?
What counts as success, failure, and inconclusive?
Will you run the original analysis, an updated one, or both?

fields.label: Primary analysis (matched to your replication goal)
fields.help: Usually the same test as the original (e.g. an independent-samples t-test), matched to your goal from Stage 2.

fields.label: Success / failure / inconclusive criteria
fields.help: Decide now what counts as success, failure and 'inconclusive'. E.g. 'Success: effect in the same direction and statistically significant. Inconclusive: confidence interval includes both zero and the original effect.'

fields.label: How you will compare with the original (e.g. CI for the difference, equivalence)
fields.help: How you will compare your result with the original's. Avoid simply comparing p-values; a confidence interval for the difference between the two effects is better.

fields.label: Secondary / updated analyses
fields.help: Any extra or updated analyses beyond the original one.

checklist.text: We defined success and failure before seeing the data
checklist.technical: Success criteria are defined before analysis

checklist.text: Our analysis matches the goal we chose in Stage 2
checklist.technical: The analysis matches the chosen replication goal

checklist.text: We don't rely only on 'significant vs. not significant'
checklist.technical: Not relying only on 'significant vs. non-significant'

checklist.text: We won't compare p-values or eyeball overlapping confidence intervals
checklist.technical: Not comparing p values or eyeballing CI overlap

checklist.text: We planned how to handle careless responders and failed manipulation checks
checklist.technical: Plan for careless responding and failed manipulation checks

resources.label: APA JARS — quantitative replication reporting table

intro: Choose the analysis that answers your Stage 2 goal and decide, before seeing any data, what result would count as a successful replication, a failed replication, or an inconclusive one. 'Significant versus not significant' on its own is not a good test of whether a replication worked.

title: Interpret, report & publish
goal: Interpret the results fairly, report everything openly, invite the original authors to comment, and find the right outlet.
questions: What does the evidence, taken as a whole, say?
Which explanations for divergence are plausible, and testable?
How will you frame the paper constructively?

fields.label: Outcome in balanced language (vs. your pre-set criteria)
fields.help: Describe the outcome against your pre-set criteria, in neutral words (e.g. 'did not find evidence for' rather than 'failed').

fields.label: Possible reasons for divergence (validity, differences, moderators)
fields.help: If your results differ from the original: possible reasons such as measurement, differences in sample or setting, or chance.

fields.label: Contribution framing (building, not attacking)
fields.help: How your study adds to knowledge, rather than criticising the original authors.

fields.label: Open materials, data and code; where results will be logged
fields.help: Where you will share materials, data and code (e.g. OSF), and logging your result in FReD.

fields.label: Target outlet(s) and preprint plan
fields.help: Which journal(s) you will target, and whether you will post a preprint.

checklist.text: We describe the outcome in neutral, balanced language
checklist.technical: Uses balanced, descriptive language about the outcome

checklist.text: We carefully considered reasons for any differences from the original
checklist.technical: Evaluates reasons for divergence carefully

checklist.text: We share our materials, data and code openly
checklist.technical: Reports comprehensively and openly (materials, data, code)

checklist.text: We invited the original authors to comment on our results
checklist.technical: Original authors invited to comment on results

checklist.text: We logged our result in the FORRT Replication Database (FReD)
checklist.technical: Results logged in FReD

checklist.text: We don't treat one replication as the final word
checklist.technical: Does not treat one replication as conclusive

intro: After you have collected and analysed your data: describe the results fairly and calmly, consider possible reasons for any differences from the original, share your materials and data, and invite the original authors to comment. At the summit you can read this stage but you will complete it later.
